questions.q: Ethylamine is warmed with CS₂ and then heated with HgCl₂. The compound responsible for the mustard-oil smell is:
questions.explain: The final product is ethyl isothiocyanate, R–N=C=S. C₂H₅NHCSSH is only the dithiocarbamic acid intermediate, and C₂H₅N≡C is the isocyanide of the carbylamine test.

questions.q: Which amine gives a positive Hofmann mustard oil test?
questions.explain: Only primary amines give an isothiocyanate. Secondary amines form a dithiocarbamic acid but cannot go further, and tertiary amines do not even form the dithiocarbamic acid.

questions.q: The function of HgCl₂ in the mustard oil reaction is to:
options: Act as the electrophile that adds to the amine
Oxidise the amine to a nitro compound
Supply the carbon of the N=C=S group
Remove the elements of H₂S from the dithiocarbamic acid as black HgS
questions.explain: HgCl₂ binds strongly to sulphur and traps H₂S as HgS, leaving R–N=C=S: RNH–C(=S)–SH + HgCl₂ → R–N=C=S + HgS + 2HCl. CS₂, not HgCl₂, is the electrophile and the source of the carbon.

questions.q: Dimethylamine reacts with CS₂ but gives no mustard-oil smell after heating with HgCl₂. The reason is that:
options: Its dithiocarbamic acid (CH₃)₂N–CS–SH has no N–H left to lose when forming N=C
It does not react with CS₂ at all
It is too weak a base to attack CS₂
HgCl₂ oxidises it to a nitrosamine
questions.explain: Two N–H hydrogens are needed: one is used when the amine adds to CS₂ and the second is lost when N=C=S forms. A secondary amine has only one, so it stops at the dithiocarbamic acid.
